items.readable_text:
Content:
Euler's formula allows us to convert between complex exponential functions and complex numbers expressed in polar form. It states that

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm{i}\theta} = \cos\theta + \textrm{i}\sin\theta.]

Content:
With Euler's formula, we can write any complex number [MATH: z] in three equivalent ways. Letting [MATH: r=|z|] and [MATH: \theta =\textrm{arg}(z),] we have the following:

Content:
| | Cartesian | Polar | Exponential |
| [MATH: z] | [MATH: x+\textrm{i}y] | [MATH: r\left( \cos\theta + \textrm{i}\sin\theta\right)] | [MATH: re^{\textrm{i}\theta}] |

Content:
For instance, if [MATH: z=1+\textrm{i},] then we have
[MATH: r|= sqrt(1^{2} + 1^{2}) = sqrt(2),; θ|= arg(z) = \arctan ((1)/(1)) = (π)/(4).]

Content:
So, the complex number [MATH: z=1+\textrm{i}] can be written in exponential form as

Content:
[MATH: z=\sqrt{2}e^{\textrm{i}\pi/4}.]

Content:
When [MATH: \theta=\pi,] we have a special case:

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm{i}\pi} = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^{\textrm{i}\pi} +1=0]

Content:
The equation [MATH: e^{\textrm{i}\pi} +1=0] is called Euler's identity. It is often described as the most beautiful equation in all of mathematics because it combines five important constants [MATH: e, \textrm{i}, \pi, 1,] and [MATH: 0] into a single elegant form.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To write our complex number in the form [MATH: z = r\textrm{e}^{\textrm{i}\theta},] where [MATH: r=|z|] and [MATH: \theta = \arg(z),] we first calculate [MATH: r\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: r =|z||= sqrt(x^{2} + y^{2}); = sqrt(4^{2} + 4^{2}); = 4sqrt(2)]

Since [MATH: z] lies in the first quadrant of the complex plane, we have [MATH: θ = \arg (z)|= \arctan ((y)/(x)); = \arctan (1); = (π)/(4).]

Finally, substituting [MATH: r=4\sqrt{2}] and [MATH: \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}] into [MATH: z=re^{\textrm{i}\theta},] we get [MATH: z = 4\sqrt{2}\,\textrm{e}^{\pi\textrm{i}/4}.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
We can use Euler's formula to construct straightforward proofs of some trigonometric identities.

Content:
For example, let's prove the following:
[MATH: \cos(x+y) = \cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin y, \qquad \sin(x+y) = \sin x\cos y + \cos x\sin y]

Content:
By the rules of exponents, we have that

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm i (x+y)} = e^{\textrm i x} \cdot e^{\textrm iy}.]

Content:
Using Euler's formula, this can be written as
[MATH: \underbrace{\cos(x+y) + \textrm i\sin(x+y)}_{e^{\textrm i (x+y)} } = \underbrace{\left(\cos x + \textrm i\sin x\right)}_{e^{\textrm i x}}\cdot \underbrace{\left(\cos y + \textrm i\sin y\right)}_{e^{\textrm iy}}.]

Content:
If we expand the parentheses on the right-hand side and group real and imaginary parts, we get

Content:
[MATH: \cos (x + y) + \textrm{i}\sin (x + y)|= (\cos x + \textrm{i}\sin x) ⋅ (\cos y + \textrm{i}\sin y); = \cos x\cos y + \textrm{i}\cos x\sin y + \textrm{i}\sin x\cos y + \textrm{i}^{2}\sin x\sin y; = \cos x\cos y + \textrm{i}\cos x\sin y + \textrm{i}\sin x\cos y − \sin x\sin y; = \cos x\cos y − \sin x\sin y + \textrm{i}(\cos x\sin y + \sin x\cos y).]

Content:
So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \cos(x+y) + \textrm i\sin(x+y) = \cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin y + \textrm i\left(\cos x\sin y + \sin x\cos y\right).]

Content:
Equating the real parts of this equation gives
[MATH: \cos(x+y) = \cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin y]

Content:
and equating the imaginary parts gives

Content:
[MATH: \sin(x+y) = \sin x\cos y + \cos x\sin y]
as required.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Euler's formula allows us to convert between complex exponential functions and complex numbers expressed in polar form. It states that

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm{i}\theta} = \cos\theta + \textrm{i}\sin\theta.]

Content:
With Euler's formula, we can write any complex number [MATH: z] in three equivalent ways. Letting [MATH: r=|z|] and [MATH: \theta =\textrm{arg}(z),] we have the following:

Content:
| | Cartesian | Polar | Exponential |
| [MATH: z] | [MATH: x+\textrm{i}y] | [MATH: r\left( \cos\theta + \textrm{i}\sin\theta\right)] | [MATH: re^{\textrm{i}\theta}] |

Content:
For instance, if [MATH: z=1+\textrm{i},] then we have
[MATH: r|= sqrt(1^{2} + 1^{2}) = sqrt(2),; θ|= arg(z) = \arctan ((1)/(1)) = (π)/(4).]

Content:
So, the complex number [MATH: z=1+\textrm{i}] can be written in exponential form as

Content:
[MATH: z=\sqrt{2}e^{\textrm{i}\pi/4}.]

Content:
When [MATH: \theta=\pi,] we have a special case:

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm{i}\pi} = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^{\textrm{i}\pi} +1=0]

Content:
The equation [MATH: e^{\textrm{i}\pi} +1=0] is called Euler's identity. It is often described as the most beautiful equation in all of mathematics because it combines five important constants [MATH: e, \textrm{i}, \pi, 1,] and [MATH: 0] into a single elegant form.

---

Item 2 — Example: Writing a Complex Number in Exponential Form

Example Prompt:
Write the complex number [MATH: z=4+4\textrm{i}] in exponential form.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To write our complex number in the form [MATH: z = r\textrm{e}^{\textrm{i}\theta},] where [MATH: r=|z|] and [MATH: \theta = \arg(z),] we first calculate [MATH: r\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: r =|z||= sqrt(x^{2} + y^{2}); = sqrt(4^{2} + 4^{2}); = 4sqrt(2)]

Since [MATH: z] lies in the first quadrant of the complex plane, we have
[MATH: θ = \arg (z)|= \arctan ((y)/(x)); = \arctan (1); = (π)/(4).]

Finally, substituting [MATH: r=4\sqrt{2}] and [MATH: \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}] into [MATH: z=re^{\textrm{i}\theta},] we get
[MATH: z = 4\sqrt{2}\,\textrm{e}^{\pi\textrm{i}/4}.]

[IMG: /graphics/a0fe46e109e3784d66675d033d5fdbd8]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The complex number shown in the Argand diagram can be written as

[MATH: z|= x + \textrm{i}y; = − 3 + 2\textrm{i}.]

To write it in the form [MATH: z = r\textrm{e}^{\textrm{i}\theta},] where [MATH: r=|z|] and [MATH: \theta = \arg(z),] we first calculate [MATH: r\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: r =|z||= sqrt(x^{2} + y^{2}); = sqrt((− 3)^{2} + 2^{2}); = sqrt(13)]

Now, since [MATH: z] lies in the second quadrant, we can find the angle [MATH: \theta] as
[MATH: \arg (z)|= π −|\arctan ((y)/(x))|; = π −|\arctan ((2)/(3))|; = π − 0.588; = 2.554]

to three decimal places.

Finally, substituting [MATH: r=\sqrt{13}] and [MATH: \theta=2.554] into [MATH: z=re^{\textrm{i} \theta},] we get
[MATH: z = \sqrt{13}\,\textrm{e}^{2.554\,\textrm{i}}\,.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Proving the Sum Formulas for Sine and Cosine

Content:
We can use Euler's formula to construct straightforward proofs of some trigonometric identities.

Content:
For example, let's prove the following:
[MATH: \cos(x+y) = \cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin y, \qquad \sin(x+y) = \sin x\cos y + \cos x\sin y]

Content:
By the rules of exponents, we have that

Content:
[MATH: e^{\textrm i (x+y)} = e^{\textrm i x} \cdot e^{\textrm iy}.]

Content:
Using Euler's formula, this can be written as
[MATH: \underbrace{\cos(x+y) + \textrm i\sin(x+y)}_{e^{\textrm i (x+y)} } = \underbrace{\left(\cos x + \textrm i\sin x\right)}_{e^{\textrm i x}}\cdot \underbrace{\left(\cos y + \textrm i\sin y\right)}_{e^{\textrm iy}}.]

Content:
If we expand the parentheses on the right-hand side and group real and imaginary parts, we get

Content:
[MATH: \cos (x + y) + \textrm{i}\sin (x + y)|= (\cos x + \textrm{i}\sin x) ⋅ (\cos y + \textrm{i}\sin y); = \cos x\cos y + \textrm{i}\cos x\sin y + \textrm{i}\sin x\cos y + \textrm{i}^{2}\sin x\sin y; = \cos x\cos y + \textrm{i}\cos x\sin y + \textrm{i}\sin x\cos y − \sin x\sin y; = \cos x\cos y − \sin x\sin y + \textrm{i}(\cos x\sin y + \sin x\cos y).]

Content:
So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \cos(x+y) + \textrm i\sin(x+y) = \cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin y + \textrm i\left(\cos x\sin y + \sin x\cos y\right).]

Content:
Equating the real parts of this equation gives
[MATH: \cos(x+y) = \cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin y]

Content:
and equating the imaginary parts gives

Content:
[MATH: \sin(x+y) = \sin x\cos y + \cos x\sin y]
as required.
